PUBLIC SERVICE DATA · 2025

Staffing fairness and barriers: 2025 survey

What federal employees reported about staffing fairness, bias, assessment and accommodation in the 2025 Staffing and Non-Partisanship Survey (SNPS). These findings describe respondents across organizations subject to the Public Service Employment Act. They are not results for any one department.

Who answered? 82,987 respondents, with a 30.9% response rate. Surveyed June 5 to August 14, 2025. Questions about past staffing experiences generally refer to April 1, 2024 through March 31, 2025. Results are adjusted for non-response. PSC 2025 report ↗
45%said staffing processes in their department or agency reduce or eliminate biases and barriers (55% in 2023)
15%of advertised-process participants reported being disadvantaged by biases or barriers (18% in 2023)
76%agreed that selection of someone for a position is done fairly (77% in 2023)
71%agreed that non-advertised appointments are done fairly (new question in 2025)

Who reported being disadvantaged by biases or barriers in an advertised staffing process?

Percentage of respondents who participated in an advertised staffing process and answered Yes to experiencing biases or barriers that disadvantaged them. This is not the percentage of all public servants.

Source: Public Service Commission, 2025 SNPS report, Table 16. Weighted survey percentages. Group results may overlap.

Assessment accommodation and accessibility

For employees who requested assessment accommodation, 72% of employees with disabilities reported receiving it, compared with 45% of employees without disabilities. Separately, 10% of employees with disabilities reported needing an accommodation but not requesting one, compared with 1% of employees without disabilities. These figures refer to different respondent groups, not all employees.

Source: PSC 2025 SNPS report, Table 13.

What these results can and cannot show: Survey differences help identify questions to investigate. They do not establish individual discrimination or a causal mechanism. The 2025 SNPS examines staffing processes and political impartiality; it is distinct from the 2024 Public Service Employee Survey. No custom theme weights or overall equity scores are calculated here.

What this tool can show
  • Representation gaps against workforce availability
  • Disproportionate harm in the survey, by group
  • Likely locations of barriers, to investigate
  • Change between survey cycles
  • Where data is missing or suppressed
  • Questions an organization should be able to answer

What it cannot prove on its own
  • That any individual was discriminated against
  • Causation, that one thing caused another
  • That an organization broke the law
  • Intent
  • The full workforce reality where self-identification is incomplete
  • Anything about groups whose counts are suppressed

What you can find out

Pick whichever question matches what you came for; the link takes you straight there.

  • How does my department compare to the public service, or to a similar-sized one? → Departments
  • How is a specific group or subgroup (say, Black employees or persons with disabilities) doing? → Groups & subgroups
  • Are people being paid equitably, and does "visible minority" hide differences? → Salary and Salary DI tracker
  • Where do people fall out of hiring and promotion? → Hiring & promotion
  • What did employees say about discrimination, harassment and advancement? → Employee survey
  • Who reaches the executive ranks? → Executives
  • What's the case for employee support services, and how do organizations compare? → Support services
  • How do I ask for data that isn't public, with the right legal backing? → Take action

Getting around
  • Tabs across the top are the sections. On a phone they wrap onto more than one row; scroll up to see them all. You can also move between them with the arrow keys.
  • Switching scope. Most pages let you choose the whole public service, a single department, or a specific group, using the dropdowns and buttons near the top of each page.
  • Getting data out. Every table has a Copy button (pastes into Excel) and a CSV button (downloads the table). Every section has a Print / Save as PDF button for briefing notes.

How to read what you see

Five things explain almost every chart and table in the tool.

  • Bars with a vertical line through them. The bar is the actual number; the short vertical line is the benchmark (usually workforce availability, the share you'd expect). If the bar stops short of the line, the group is below the benchmark; if it pushes past, it's above.
  • Red means below, green means at or above. A red number or bar is a prompt to look closer, never a conclusion on its own.
  • Ratios. A ratio of 1.0 means a group got exactly its proportional share (of promotions, of a pay band, and so on). Below 1.0 means less than its share; above 1.0 means more.
  • "supp." means suppressed. When a count is 1 to 5 people it's hidden to protect privacy. It is not zero, it's just too small to publish.
  • Percentages are a group's share, for example "23.9% racialized" means 23.9% of those employees self-identified as a member of a visible minority.

Where a number comes from is labelled:

official data transcribed directly from TBS, the PSC or the survey.   computed a ratio, gap or ranking worked out from official figures.   you enter values you type into a calculator or comparator.   interpretation a possible barrier or hypothesis to test, never a finding.

What each tab does

Grouped by what you're trying to do.

See where groups stand

  • Overview — the headline numbers and the strongest barrier signals, each linked to the detail.
  • Departments — representation for each organization; rank them, search, or compare two side by side.
  • Groups & subgroups — each published subgroup, with trends since 2018 and its leadership gap.

Find the barriers

  • Salary — who sits in which pay band, and the differences hidden inside "visible minority".
  • Hiring & promotion — hires, promotions and separations, plus the recruitment funnel stage by stage.
  • Executives — representation in the executive ranks, by level, against each group's share of the workforce.
  • Salary DI tracker — the Disproportionality Index over 2017 to 2025, showing pay compression year by year.

Hear from people, and see the context

  • Employee survey — 2024 PSES results on discrimination, harassment, racism and advancement.
  • Where people work — region, occupation, language and intersectionality, the context behind the other numbers.

Act on it

  • Support services — the data case for employee networks, an ombuds office, conflict management and anti-racism teams, a cost calculator, and a comparator that groups organizations by size.
  • Linkages lab — connects datasets to raise barriers no single table shows, with a relationship explorer and a finding builder.
  • Take action — legal references, key release dates, and a generator that writes a formal data request for what isn't public.

Check the data itself

  • Data files — where each dataset lives, for pulling figures directly.
  • Data sources — the full source list, noting what's embedded here versus in a live dashboard.
  • About the data — definitions (workforce availability, suppression, the ratios) and the honest limits.

Three cautions to keep in mind
  1. These are screening signals, not findings. A red flag tells you where to look, not that something is wrong. Each organization has its own workforce availability reflecting its jobs and location, so a gap against the public-service average is a reason to investigate, not a verdict.
  2. The numbers can undercount. Self-identification is voluntary, so real representation may be higher than shown, and when trust is low people self-identify less, exactly where problems may be worst.
  3. Some data is linked, not embedded. Departmental promotions, acting appointments, subgroup-by-department figures and per-department survey results live in interactive federal dashboards; the tool links you straight to them.

Overview

Key signals across the public service interpretation

The most defensible barrier signals in the data, each linked to the section where you can verify it. These are screening signals drawn from published figures, not findings of non-compliance; the value is knowing where to look.

  1. The executive cliff for racialized employees. 23.9% of the workforce but 17.3% of executives; for Black employees, 5.1% of the workforce but 3.2% of executives. See Executives.
  2. Pay compression for Black employees. A disproportionality index of 1.46 in the lowest salary range and 0.63 in the highest in 2025, with an estimated median-salary gap of $10,450. See Salary DI tracker.
  3. The recruitment funnel sheds three of four groups. Persons with disabilities fall from 4.4% of applicants to 2.4% of appointments; Black candidates from 10.3% to 6.6%. Automated screening costs no representation; the human stages do. See Hiring & promotion.
  4. Disability is the one group below availability, and slipping. Representation at 9.0% against a 12.0% benchmark, accommodation implementation down from 81% to 71%, disability-based discrimination the fastest-rising type. See Groups & subgroups.
  5. The formal complaint system has lost people's trust. 75% of discrimination comes from those with authority, 53% take no action, and only 11% of race-discrimination victims are satisfied with how complaints are resolved. See Ombuds value.
  6. "Visible minority" hides opposite realities. Among those earning $100K+, Chinese employees sit at 47.4% and Filipino employees at 21.4%; the group average conceals both. See Salary.

This tool is for every public servant, anyone in any department or agency who wants to see where equity groups stand and where they may face barriers in hiring, promotion, pay and leadership. All figures are transcribed from published Government of Canada tables, with nothing estimated. Suppressed small counts stay suppressed.

What lives here and what lives in the dashboards. This site embeds the complete published TBS tables: representation by department, subgroups, salary, hiring, promotion, separations, executives, regions, occupations and languages. Departmental promotions, acting appointments, applicant data by subgroup and PSES results are served by interactive federal dashboards that cannot be copied wholesale; every section links you straight to the right dashboard, pre-pointed at your department where the dashboard allows it. Public-service-wide 2024 PSES results for every equity question are embedded in the Employee survey section, with per-organization pages one link away. New here? Open the How to use this tab first.

A department far below the line is a screening signal, not a finding: departmental availability differs by occupation mix and region, so use this to decide where to look closer.

The long arc, 1998 to 2025

Representation of all four designated groups in the core public administration over 27 years. Progress is real and slow, which is exactly why barrier-level data matters.

How the benchmark itself has moved: workforce availability by census era
Workforce availability estimates over time. The 2016-to-2021 jumps for persons with disabilities and racialized people reflect both real population change and definitional changes (expanded disability definition; permanent residents included from 2021).
Census eraWomenIndigenousDisabilitiesRacialized
1991 (Census + HALS)47.3%2.6%4.8%9.0%
199648.7%1.7%4.8%8.7%
200152.2%2.5%3.6%10.4%
2006 (+ PALS)52.3%3.0%4.0%12.4%
2011 (NHS + CSD 2012)52.5%3.4%4.4%13.0%
2016 (citizens only, CSD 2017)52.7%4.0%9.0%15.3%
2021 (citizens + permanent residents, CSD 2022)54.9%4.0%12.0%22.7%

Why this matters for barrier arguments: meeting a benchmark that itself lags the population is a moving target, and TBS describes WFA as a starting point rather than a ceiling. The 2021 inclusion of permanent residents raised the racialized availability by 7.4 points overnight, instantly reframing which organizations look on track.

Three patterns the data already shows

First, the executive cliff for racialized employees: 23.9% of the workforce but 17.3% of executives, and for Black employees 5.1% of the workforce but 3.2% of executives. Second, salary compression for Black employees: 40.8% earn between $50,000 and $74,999 compared with 27.9% of all employees, the pattern the Disproportionality Index study first documented. Third, the disability availability gap: representation rose to 9.0% but remains 3 points below the 12.0% availability estimate; part of that distance reflects the newer, broader survey definition of disability that the self-identification form does not yet use. Each pattern has its own section in this tool.

Departments and agencies

Representation of the four designated groups in each core public administration organization, with automatic barrier flags. The core public administration is the set of organizations where the Treasury Board is the legal employer, listed in Schedules I and IV of the Financial Administration Act; this is the full published list for the March 31, 2025 cycle, not a sample, and the count shifts slightly year to year as departments are created, merged or renamed (72 here). Separate agencies (CRA, CFIA, NRC, Parks Canada and others) are a different schedule and publish their own reports; links are in Data sources.

Salary and pay equity

Who sits where on the pay scale. The disproportionality ratio compares each group's share in a salary band with the share of all employees in that band: above 1.0 means overrepresented in the band, below 1.0 means underrepresented. Overrepresentation in low bands plus underrepresentation in high bands is the compression pattern that signals blocked progression.

How to read this

  • The bar shows the actual result.
  • The tick or benchmark shows the comparison point.
  • A result below benchmark may signal a gap.
  • Suppressed data means the count is too small to publish. It does not mean zero.
  • Read this with related data before drawing conclusions.

What this may mean

Concentration in lower salary bands may signal barriers in hiring, classification, promotion or access to acting roles.

Disproportionality ratios at a glance, all groups

Reading example: 1.46 for Black employees in the $50,000 to $74,999 band means Black employees are 46% more concentrated in that band than the workforce as a whole.

Computed from TBS published salary distributions, March 31, 2025. Method: Disproportionality Index (Albury, Vongdara, Nicholas, Kanji).

Who holds each pay band

A different cut of the same data: out of everyone in a band, what share belongs to each group. The tick is the group's share of the whole workforce, so a bar falling short of its tick in the top bands shows the pay ceiling directly. Women are 68.5% of the under $50K band but 47.5% of the $125K to $149,999 band. Middle-band values are computed from the published band counts and verified against published totals.

Subgroup salary distributions

TBS publishes subgroup salary in four bands. Compare the share earning $100,000 and over: 41.5% of all employees, 47.4% of Chinese employees, 28.5% of Black employees, 21.4% of Filipino employees. Same group label, very different realities, which is exactly why subgroup data matters.

Hiring, promotion and separation

Who gets in, who moves up, and who leaves, public-service-wide, for nine fiscal years. A group's promotion share below its workforce share signals a promotion barrier; a rising separation share signals a retention problem worth disaggregating from retirements.

Hiring, promotions and separations

Before hiring: the recruitment funnel, stage by stage

The PSC's Audit of Employment Equity Representation in Recruitment followed 15,285 applications to 181 externally advertised processes across 30 organizations through all five hiring stages. It is the only published dataset showing exactly where each group falls out of the funnel. The survival ratio is appointment-stage representation divided by application-stage representation: 1.00 means a group ends where it started; below 1.00 means the process itself shed them.

Representation at each recruitment stage (audit sample, processes closing 2016-17, published 2021). Source: PSC audit, Annex B.
GroupApplicationAutomated screeningOrganizational screeningAssessmentAppointmentSurvival ratio
Women52.8%53.2%59.7%59.8%58.2%1.10
Indigenous Peoples3.5%3.6%4.0%2.9%2.9%0.83
Persons with disabilities4.4%4.7%4.5%3.6%2.4%0.55
Members of visible minorities30.4%30.3%27.4%24.6%24.7%0.81
Black candidates10.3%9.7%7.7%6.3%6.6%0.64
Chinese candidates3.4%3.5%4.2%3.2%3.5%1.03
Non-white West Asian, North African or Arab4.6%4.4%3.8%4.2%3.3%0.72
South Asian / East Indian5.6%5.8%5.0%5.2%5.9%1.05

The audit named the mechanism at each stage. Automated screening cost no group representation; the losses are human. Organizational screening cut racialized candidates, Black candidates hardest, with citizenship status and how experience was judged identified as factors, and visible minority candidates less successful even when they had federal experience. At assessment, written tests (mostly organization-built, open-ended, subjectively scored) hurt racialized and especially Black candidates; interviews drove the entire Indigenous drop; reference checks helped only women. The appointment stage itself cut persons with disabilities, their largest single drop. The 2023 follow-up audit on pre-assessment found the same screening also reduced representation for intersectional candidates: Indigenous people with disabilities and racialized people with disabilities. And the accountability gap: only 50% of organizations had done an employment system review in the prior 3 to 5 years, and 62% of those concluded they had no systemic barriers, while this audit was finding them. Self-assessment is not detection.

Promotion vs acting workbench

Acting appointments are the rehearsal space for promotion, and they are the one staffing flow missing from every TBS table. Pull your organization's numbers from the PSC subgroup dashboard (it reports employees, promotions AND acting appointments by group and subgroup per organization), enter them here, and the workbench computes both equity ratios and tells you what the pattern means. A healthy acting ratio with a weak promotion ratio, or the reverse, localizes the barrier.

2024-25 equity check: share of actions vs. share of workforce

A ratio of 1.00 means the group received exactly its proportional share. Below 0.90 is flagged.

Fiscal year 2024-25. Hires 19,720, promotions 25,449, separations 15,472. Source: TBS Demographic Snapshot 2024-2025.

Employee survey (PSES 2024)

What 186,635 public servants said about discrimination, harassment, racism, advancement and wellbeing in the 2024 Public Service Employee Survey. These are the public-service-wide results for every equity-relevant question, transcribed from the published results tables, with the 2019 to 2024 history. The experience data here is the other half of the barrier picture: representation numbers show who is present, the survey shows what happens to them.

Disproportionate harm across the public service official data

Every designated group against the public-service-wide figure for each question. Red means the group fares worse than the public service overall; the number in brackets is the gap. This is the fastest way to see which groups carry more of the harm.

2024 PSES by designated group, whole public service. Source: Employment Equity derived-variable file. "Victim" rows: percent who experienced it (lower is better).

Compare one group across organizations

Choose a group and a question to see how that group fares in every organization that published the result, ranked, with the public-service figure for that group marked. This answers questions like "where do Black employees report the least trust in recourse?" or "which departments have the widest discrimination gap for persons with disabilities?"

Screening signal, not a finding. Smaller organizations have smaller group samples, so a single department's figure can swing on a few responses; weight the public-service pattern and the larger organizations more heavily.

The gap between two groups, side by side

Pick two groups to see them answer the same questions next to each other, public-service-wide, with the difference. Useful for showing, in one view, how differently the workplace lands, for example Black employees versus non-racialized employees on feeling safe to speak about racism.

2024 PSES, whole public service, two groups compared.

Systemic barrier scanner interpretation

This scans every organization, every designated group and every question at once, and surfaces the largest disproportionate-harm signals automatically, the places where a group fares notably worse than the public service, or worse than its own organization's overall result. It turns thousands of data points into a ranked shortlist of where to look first. Filter it, then copy any row into a briefing note. Each is a screening signal, not a finding.

Largest disproportionate-harm signals across the 2024 PSES by designated group. Sorted by gap size. Source: Employment Equity derived-variable file.

Source: 2024 Public Service Employee Survey, Employment Equity derived-variable dataset (Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat / Statistics Canada), via Open Government. Group labels are respondents' self-identification. "Racialized" corresponds to the Employment Equity "visible minority" category. Independent analytical tool, not a Government of Canada publication.

Employee support services and outcomes

Funded employee networks, an ombuds office, an informal conflict management system, an anti-racism or IDEA team: these are the structures organizations use to surface and resolve workplace problems. This page makes the data case for them and lets you compare organizations by the services they offer. The argument is usually made with values; here it is made with numbers, the 2024 survey shows, in the public service's own words, where the formal system loses people, which is the gap these services exist to close.

How to read this

  • The bar shows the actual result.
  • The tick or benchmark shows the comparison point.
  • A result below benchmark may signal a gap.
  • Suppressed data means the count is too small to publish. It does not mean zero.
  • Read this with related data before drawing conclusions.

What this may mean

What these services are

An ombuds office is an independent, impartial, confidential and informal channel for raising and resolving concerns outside the chain of command. Funded employee networks give equity-seeking staff a collective voice and a route to leadership. An informal conflict management system (ICMS) is required of every deputy head under section 207 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act. An anti-racism or IDEA team or secretariat carries dedicated capacity for systemic change. Many of the survey questions below speak to all of them, not the ombuds alone.

The formal-system gap, measured

Every figure below is a verified 2024 PSES public-service-wide result from the Employee survey section. Read them as one sequence: people experience harm, mostly from those with power over them, then do not use the formal system because they fear it or do not believe in it.

The escalation funnel the formal system loses. Source: 2024 PSES, public service wide.
StageWhat the data says2024Why support services matter here
Harm occursVictim of harassment (12%) or discrimination (9%) in the past 12 months~1 in 9Demand exists in every organization, every year
Power asymmetryDiscrimination came from individuals with authority75%People will not raise issues through a chain of command that contains the problem; an ombuds or ICMS sits outside it
SilenceDiscrimination victims who took no action at all53%Unraised issues do not disappear; they convert into disengagement, sick leave and exits
FearDid not file because they feared reprisal (harassment 47%, discrimination 45%)~46%Confidentiality is the feature of an ombuds or informal channel that directly neutralizes reprisal fear
FutilityDid not file because they believed it would change nothing (harassment 57%, discrimination 65%)57-65%An informal channel with visible outcomes rebuilds the belief that raising issues works
Recourse distrustFeel they could start a formal recourse process without fear of reprisal51%Half the workforce does not trust the front door; informal services are the side door
Accountability failureRace-discrimination victims satisfied with how racism complaints are resolved11%The strongest single argument that the current resolution machinery is not working for racialized employees; the gap an anti-racism team and networks exist to close
Systemic blindnessCall to Action seen as having had a positive impact (36% answered don't know)43%Aggregated reporting from an ombuds, networks or an IDEA secretariat is one of the few mechanisms that surfaces systemic issues upward without identifying individuals

The statutory anchor: section 207 of the Federal Public Sector Labour Relations Act requires every deputy head to establish an informal conflict management system in consultation with bargaining agents; an ombuds office is the most developed form of that obligation. The pattern data these services aggregate also feeds the Employment Equity Act section 5 duty to identify and eliminate barriers, and hazard prevention obligations under Canada Labour Code Part II.

The Justice evaluation noted that a comparably sized department had three conflict-resolution practitioners while Justice had none, illustrating how unevenly these services are resourced.

Build the financial case: an interactive calculator you enter

Starting values are the official benchmarks from the evaluations above (manager time lost to conflict, replacement cost at 150% of compensation). The default cost per employee, $125,000, is the Parliamentary Budget Officer's average personnel cost per full-time equivalent (salary plus standard compensation; the PBO reports total federal personnel spending of $71.1 billion in 2024-25). Average base salary across the service is roughly $100,000 (Treasury Board). Replace any value with your own organization's figures. The model uses two conservative, direct mechanisms: time recovered from unresolved conflict, and the cost differential when matters resolve informally instead of formally. Indirect effects (turnover avoided, sick leave, legal exposure) are deliberately excluded so the result survives scrutiny.

Every assumption is visible and editable, which is the point: bring your organization's grievance counts, your ICMS intake data and your own salary mix, and the model becomes evidence rather than estimate.

3. Do groups report different experiences where they make up more of the workforce?

Each dot is one organization. Its position from left to right is the group's share of that organization's workforce (Treasury Board, March 31, 2025). Its height is the group's result on one 2024 PSES question in the same organization. By default, the height is the gap between the group and a comparison group in the same organization, for example Black respondents compared with non-racialized respondents. The gap removes differences that affect everyone in an organization, such as frontline work where harassment is common for all staff. Use this view to see whether a group fares better or worse where it makes up more of the workforce, and to find organizations far from the others. Treat any pattern as a question to look into. It does not show that one thing causes another.

Show the figures for each organization

Read with care

  • Each dot is an organization. A pattern across organizations does not tell you what any one employee experienced.
  • Results that are not published, usually because too few people are in the group, are left out. The number of organizations shown appears with every result.
  • Each organization counts once in the averages and in the pattern, whatever its size.
  • Representation comes from voluntary self-identification. Where people feel safer, more of them may self-identify, which can raise the measured share.
  • The survey results are from the 2024 PSES and representation is as of March 31, 2025. Separate agencies, such as the Canada Revenue Agency, are not in the Treasury Board representation tables, so they do not appear here.

Real progress, or just optics?

Representation can rise while the gap to the benchmark widens, because the benchmark itself moved. In 2023 the workforce-availability benchmark was updated to the 2021 Census and, for the first time, counts both Canadian citizens and permanent residents. For racialized (visible minority) employees that raised the bar substantially. A department whose representation held steady can now sit further behind, and one that posted a gain can still have lost ground against the higher benchmark. This page shows the full picture so a moved goalpost is not mistaken for a win.

How to read this

  • The bar shows the actual result.
  • The tick or benchmark shows the comparison point.
  • A result below benchmark may signal a gap.
  • Suppressed data means the count is too small to publish. It does not mean zero.
  • Read this with related data before drawing conclusions.

What this may mean

Representation can rise while the gap widens if the benchmark moved; check the gap, not just the headcount.

Check next

Overview · Salary DI tracker · Demographic gaps · Use this finding in a briefing or request →

What changed, and why it matters official data

  • The benchmark for equitable representation is workforce availability (WFA), the share of the workforce, in occupations matching the public service, that belongs to each group.
  • Until recently WFA was based on the 2016 Census and counted Canadian citizens only. It is now based on the 2021 Census and counts citizens and permanent residents (Treasury Board, March 2024 reporting).
  • For racialized employees this moved the bar up by roughly six to seven points, to 22.7%. The change reflects a more recent count and a broader, fairer population, not a failure by any single department, but it does mean year-over-year representation cannot be read on its own.
  • The honest test is not "did our number go up?" but "did our gap to the current benchmark close?" The two can move in opposite directions.

Racialized representation against the current (raised) benchmark

Each organization's racialized representation against the 22.7% public-service workforce-availability benchmark. Red sits below it. Many organizations that look healthy on a raw representation number are below the benchmark once the bar is set where it now stands. Sort and filter to see who is genuinely at parity.

How to talk about it honestly

If your organization's racialized representation rose but is still below 22.7%, the accurate statement is that representation improved and a gap to workforce availability remains. If it rose and the benchmark rose faster, say so. Claiming parity because a raw number climbed, when the gap to the current benchmark persists, is the optics trap this page exists to prevent. The same caution applies in reverse: a department that looks worse against the new benchmark has not necessarily regressed; the bar moved.

Sources: Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat, employment-equity representation and workforce-availability estimates (2021 Census and 2022 Canadian Survey on Disability, citizens and permanent residents, as of March 31, 2024 and 2025). The benchmark change is documented in TBS employment-equity reporting. Independent analytical tool.

Language and advancement

Bilingualism is a gate to advancement in the public service: most executive positions carry a bilingual requirement, and access to second-language training is not evenly available. That makes language an equity issue, especially where a group is more likely to work in its second official language or to face discrimination at the same time. This page shows who reports language training and discrimination holding their careers back.

How to read this

  • The bar shows the actual result.
  • The tick or benchmark shows the comparison point.
  • A result below benchmark may signal a gap.
  • Suppressed data means the count is too small to publish. It does not mean zero.
  • Read this with related data before drawing conclusions.

What this may mean

Language requirements can act as a structural barrier to advancement for some groups; read this with promotion and executive data.

Lack of second-language training as a career barrier official data

Share of employees in each group who said, in 2024, that lack of access to training in their second official language adversely affected their career progress (to a moderate or greater extent). Higher is worse.

Discrimination as a career barrier

For context, the share in each group who said discrimination adversely affected their career progress over the same period. The two barriers often fall on the same employees.

Why this matters

Roughly half of Black employees in the federal public service report French as a first official language, well above the workforce average, so a bilingual requirement combined with uneven access to language training does not fall evenly. When the path to executive roles runs through a second-language standard, the question is whether every group has the same real chance to meet it.

The honest test for an organization: are language-training spots distributed equitably across groups and levels, and is the bilingual requirement applied in a way that opens advancement rather than narrowing it? The data here is a prompt to check, not proof on its own.

Source: 2024 Public Service Employee Survey, Employment Equity derived-variable file, question 44 (barriers to career progress), share reporting an adverse effect. Overall figure from PSES subset 1. Group labels are respondents' self-identification.

Will the gaps close on their own?

At the current share of hiring that goes to a group, most gaps do not close on their own within any timeframe worth planning around. Closing a gap takes a higher hiring share, lower attrition, or both. How long it would take cannot be projected honestly without modelling hiring, attrition and self-identification together, and the published data does not support that. So this tool puts no number of years on the question.

A gap that holds steady year after year is itself the finding: the current approach is not closing it. To see whether a gap is actually moving, use the "What changed" section and compare representation against the workforce-availability benchmark.

Where groups are made invisible

Every suppressed or unpublished cell is a place where a group is too small to appear, which is itself a finding. Small communities, and people at intersections, are the ones most often missing from the public numbers. This page counts where that happens and turns it into a request for the data that does exist internally.

Methodology and audit trail

Every figure in this tool is transcribed from a published Government of Canada source; nothing is modelled or estimated. This page records, for each dataset, where it came from, what was done to it, and what it can and cannot support, so the work can be checked and reproduced.

Principles

  • Numbers are copied verbatim from official tables. Where a value was derived (for example, summing salary bands), the calculation is noted and was checked against published totals.
  • Suppressed cells are left suppressed. They are never estimated, interpolated or filled.
  • No organization's data is matched to a different organization. Where a name could not be matched across datasets, the cell is left blank.
  • Survey gaps and correlations are screening signals, not findings. They show where to look, not what is true.

Linkages lab: find barriers you did not know about

Single datasets show gaps; barriers live in the connections between them. This page joins the datasets already in this site so patterns surface that none of them shows alone, and gives you two instruments: a relationship explorer over all 72 organizations, and a signal builder that turns thresholds into a ready-to-paste finding.

Linkages hiding in plain sight

Each row connects two or more datasets from this site to raise a question no single table answers. Use it as a menu of hypotheses to test in your own organization; the data trail is stated so you can follow it. These are leads, not conclusions. The last two draw on the new by-group survey data in the Demographic gaps tab.

Each linkage joins two or more verified datasets from this site. These are hypotheses to investigate, with the data trail stated.
LinkageThe data trail (all verified, in this site)The barrier hypothesis
The recognition paradoxBy designated group in 2024, Black employees report being a victim of discrimination at 15% and Indigenous employees at 16%, against 9% overall, yet on "feel valued at work" Black employees sit at 69%, near the overall 67%. Persons with disabilities report discrimination at 21% and feeling valued at only 59%.Harm and belonging are not the same axis; a group can be both engaged and discriminated against, which means engagement scores can mask discrimination. Test: never read a high "valued" or engagement score as evidence that discrimination is low; check the discrimination items separately by group.
The silencing of the most affectedBlack employees report feeling safe to speak about racism without reprisal at 51%, against 72% overall, the widest gap of any group on that question, while also reporting the most race-based discrimination. 2SLGBTQIA+ and Indigenous employees also sit below the average on safety to speak.The groups experiencing the most harm feel least safe reporting it, so formal complaint counts will systematically understate what is happening to them. Test: pair complaint volumes with the by-group "safe to speak" figure before concluding a low complaint count means low harm.
The language ladder48.5% of Black employees have French as their first official language (vs 30.2% average). 34% say lack of access to second-language training hurt their career. Executive positions are overwhelmingly bilingual-imperative.Access to language training functions as a hidden promotion gate, and it gates Black francophone employees hardest. Test: compare language-training allocation by EE group in your organization.
The disability triple bindThe only group below availability (9.0% vs 12.0%). Accommodation implementation fell from 81% to 71% while requests rose by half. Disability discrimination as a cited type jumped from 19% to 26%, the fastest of any ground. Separation share rose from 6.6% to 8.7%.Recruitment, accommodation and retention are failing simultaneously; fixing only hiring will fill a leaking bucket. Test: track accommodation request-to-implementation time alongside separations.
The untracked acting pipelinePublic-service-wide promotion shares now meet or exceed workforce shares for all four groups, yet belief in promotion fell to 51% and 25% report discrimination harmed their career. Acting appointments, the main feeder to promotion, are the one staffing flow not in any TBS table; only the PSC dashboard reports them, and the National Joint Council's equity committee flagged them for consultation.The promotion barrier has likely moved upstream into who gets acting opportunities and at what level promotions happen. Test: pull acting shares by group and subgroup from the PSC dashboard for your organization.
Geography shapes everythingRacialized representation runs from 5.1% in PEI to 31.1% in BC; Indigenous representation from 2.8% in Quebec to 53.0% in Nunavut; Black representation is 6.7% in Quebec but 1.1% in BC. Departments concentrate in different regions.Comparing organizations without their regional and occupational mix penalizes the wrong ones and excuses the wrong ones; insist on each organization's own WFA, not the national line. The explorer below makes the mix visible.
The occupational segregation engineWomen are 74.0% of administrative support but 21.7% of operational services and 7.2% of electronics. Racialized employees are 37.8% of comptrollership but 8.2% of operational services. The salary section shows the result: pay gaps emerge with no within-band discrimination at all.Classification and occupational streaming is the quiet machine behind the salary distribution. Test: track movement between categories, not just within them, and audit who enters feeder classifications.
Trust collapse corrupts the data itselfSelf-identification is voluntary. Feeling safe to speak about racism fell 5 points; recourse trust fell to 51%; survey response was 50.5%.When trust falls, self-ID and survey participation fall with it, so the data understates problems exactly where they are worst. Equity data quality is itself an outcome measure. Test: monitor self-ID completion rates as a trust indicator.
The assessment machinePSC recruitment audit: automated screening cost no group representation; human stages did. Written tests (organization-built, open-ended, subjectively scored) cut racialized and especially Black candidates; interviews drove the entire Indigenous drop; reference checks helped only women; the appointment decision itself cut persons with disabilities. 88% of candidates with disabilities never requested assessment accommodation.The barrier is not "hiring" in general, it is specific tools at specific stages, which means it is fixable tool by tool: structured scoring guides, diverse boards (only 12% of organizations required one EE member), and proactive accommodation offers. Test: inventory which assessment tools your organization used in its last 20 processes.
The review that finds nothing50% of audited organizations had done an employment system review in the prior 3 to 5 years; 62% of those concluded they had no systemic recruitment barriers, in the same period the PSC's own audit was documenting stage-by-stage losses for three of four groups.Self-assessment is not detection. Employment system reviews built and graded by the system being reviewed will keep returning clean results; pair every ESR with external data like this site, the PSC dashboards and disaggregated PSES results. Test: compare your last ESR's conclusions against your organization's rows here.

Relationship explorer: does one measure track another across organizations?

What this is: a scatter plot. You choose a measure for the horizontal axis and another for the vertical, and each dot is one organization placed by its two values. How to read it: if the dots drift from bottom-left to top-right, the two measures tend to rise together; if top-left to bottom-right, one rises as the other falls; if they're a shapeless cloud, the two aren't related. The "r" value sums that up from -1 to +1 (0 means no link). What it's for: spotting a pattern worth a closer look, for example whether organizations with more racialized staff also have more at the executive level, and especially spotting the outliers that sit far off the trend. It is a starting question, never a conclusion.

Signal builder: turn a threshold into a finding

Pick a group and how far below the public-service availability counts as a flag. The builder lists every organization that trips it and writes a summary you can paste into a briefing note. Remember the caveat it includes: departmental availability differs, so these are screening signals.

Data files: where every dataset actually lives

The dashboards are windows; these are the warehouses. The PSC dashboard runs on the Treasury Board Employment Equity Data Bank (EEDB) matched against the PSC hiring and staffing activities files, and the machine-readable releases sit on the Open Government portal and canada.ca. Every file family is mapped below with direct locations, and the importer at the bottom lets this site read the official CSVs itself, in your browser, with nothing uploaded anywhere.

Take action: calendar, legal hooks, and the request that gets the data

Data becomes accountability when it arrives on schedule, attaches to an obligation, and gets asked for in writing. This page is the operating rhythm: what lands when, which legal instrument each dataset serves, and a generator that writes the formal internal data request for the things no portal publishes.

Build a request by topic

Choose a topic, an organization and a period. This writes a structured, ready-to-send request with the fields to ask for, the format, the suppression rules and the purpose. No data is invented.

Requests existing data; asserts no finding. Trim the fields to what you need.

The accountability calendar

When each dataset and report is released through the year. Use it to time requests and briefings so you are asking for data shortly after it lands, not months later.

Release rhythm of every dataset family, and the question to ask the day each one lands.
DatasetCadenceThe question to ask on arrival
PSES results and open dataAnnual cycle (2024 fielded Oct to Dec, results the following spring)Did discrimination, racism-safety and recourse-trust questions move, overall and for each demographic group, in my organization vs the public service?
TBS EE Annual Report + Demographic SnapshotAnnual (2024-25 edition published March 2026)Did my organization's representation, hires, promotions and separations move in the right direction for each group AND subgroup, and did the EX gap narrow?
SNPS open dataBiennial (2023, then 2025 released April 2026)Do EE group members in my organization perceive staffing as fair, and how does that compare with the hard promotion and acting ratios?
PSC dashboards (EE by organization, staffing)Updated periodically through the yearWhat are this year's acting appointment shares by subgroup, the one number no annual report prints?
Workforce availability estimatesCensus era (current: 2021 Census + 2022 CSD; next rebase after the 2026 Census)When the benchmark jumps, which organizations that looked on track no longer are, and is anyone pretending the old benchmark still applies?
Executive population statisticsAnnualIs EX-level progress happening above EX-01, or only at the entry door?
CHRC employment equity auditsPeriodic horizontal auditsWhich of the audit's findings describe my organization, and what is the documented management response?

Legal hook map: which obligation each dataset evidences

Links each kind of data to the law or commitment it speaks to. Use it to anchor a finding in a specific obligation, which is what moves a number from interesting to actionable.

The instruments that turn gaps into duties.
InstrumentThe obligationThe evidence in this site
Employment Equity Act, s.5Identify and eliminate employment barriers; implement positive policies; reasonable accommodationRepresentation gaps, the recruitment funnel, promotion and acting ratios, salary disproportionality
Employment Equity Act, s.21Annual reporting to Parliament through Treasury BoardThe embedded annual report tables; separate agencies report individually
Public Service Employment Act, s.36(2) (2023 amendment)Hiring managers must evaluate assessment methods for bias and barriers and make reasonable efforts to remove or mitigate themThe recruitment audit's stage-by-stage tool findings: written tests, interviews, reference checks
Canadian Human Rights Act, s.7 and s.10No discriminatory practices or policies in employment, including systemic onesPSES discrimination results by ground; the 11% resolution-satisfaction figure for racism complaints
Canada Labour Code, Part IIHazard prevention, including psychological hazards, with employer duty to investigate and preventHarassment and discrimination prevalence, psychological-health scores, the accommodation implementation slide
FPSLRA, s.207Every deputy head must establish an informal conflict management systemThe whole Ombuds value page: the recourse-fear and futility numbers are the gap an ICMS exists to close
Accessible Canada ActIdentify, remove and prevent accessibility barriers; published accessibility plansDisability funnel collapse (4.4% to 2.4%), accommodation request and implementation trends
Clerk's Call to Action (2021)Appoint, sponsor and recruit equity-seeking employees; measurable commitments by deputy headsBlack EX representation, subgroup trends, and the PSES question on whether the Call has had any visible impact (43%)

Data request generator

The most important barrier data is internal: acting by subgroup and duration, language training allocation, accommodation timelines, self-ID completion. Pick what you need and this writes the formal request, citing the right instruments and the right source systems by name, with suppression and format requirements built in.

Export as a package

Salary Disproportionality Index tracker (2017–2025)

The Disproportionality Index (DI) asks a simple question: within a given salary range, is a group present at the rate you would expect? A DI of 1.0 means a group sits in that salary range at exactly the same rate as all employees. Above 1.0 means overrepresented in that range; below 1.0 means underrepresented. The telltale sign of blocked pay progression is a group stacking up above 1.0 in the lowest ranges and dropping below 1.0 in the highest. These are the published figures from the independent Employment Equity / Disproportionality Index project, which derives them from TBS Diversity and Inclusion statistics.

How to read this

  • The bar shows the actual result.
  • The tick or benchmark shows the comparison point.
  • A result below benchmark may signal a gap.
  • Suppressed data means the count is too small to publish. It does not mean zero.
  • Read this with related data before drawing conclusions.

What this may mean

A ratio below 1.0 in higher bands, or above 1.0 in lower bands, may signal blocked pay progression for a group.

Check next

Salary · Hiring and promotion · Executives · Use this finding in a briefing or request →

DI for a group in a salary range = (that group's % in the range) ÷ (all employees' % in the same range). Example from the source: in 2024, 34.78% of Black employees but 23.87% of all employees earned in the lowest range, giving a DI of 34.78 ÷ 23.87 = 1.46. Salary ranges shift year to year because they track the median; the source re-bins each year, which is why the band labels below change with the year you pick.

Full DI table, selected year

Every group, every salary range, percent and DI side by side. Bold red marks DI at or below 0.85 (notably underrepresented) in the upper ranges or at or above 1.15 (notably overrepresented) in the lower ranges, the two signatures of compression.

Estimated median salary by group, 2017–2025

The DI is built on these medians. The dollar gap between the all-employee line and each group line is the bottom line of pay equity. Black employees' median has trailed the overall median every year and the dollar gap has widened, not closed.

All employeesBlackVisible minorityIndigenousPersons with disabilities

The widening gap, in dollars

All-employee median minus each group's median, by year. Rising bars mean the pay gap is growing in absolute dollars even when representation counts improve, the distinction between getting in the door and getting paid equally.

Black vs non-racialized DI disparity, 2025

This is the source project's headline measure: in each salary range, the DI of non-visible-minority employees minus the DI of Black employees. Bars above zero in low ranges and below zero in high ranges show Black employees concentrated low and absent high, persistently across nine years.

Source: independent Employment Equity / Disproportionality Index repository CSVs, 2017–2025, retrieved October 26, 2026 and checked against the Drive files. Medians are grouped-data estimates rounded to $50. Imputed cells in 2019–2022 are not observed TBS counts. The 2025 band boundaries were checked against the underlying salary counts.

About the data

Definitions you need

Core public administration (CPA)
The 72 organizations where Treasury Board is the employer. Separate agencies such as CRA, CFIA, NRC and Parks Canada have their own reports.
Workforce availability (WFA)
The estimated share of each designated group in the Canadian workforce who could be recruited into public service jobs, based on the 2021 Census and 2022 Canadian Survey on Disability. It is the legal benchmark under the Employment Equity Act, and TBS itself calls it a starting point, not a ceiling.
Representation
The share of employees who have voluntarily self-identified with a group. Because self-identification is voluntary, true numbers may be higher than reported.
Designated groups
Women, Indigenous Peoples, persons with disabilities, and members of visible minorities (racialized employees), as set in the Employment Equity Act. Black employees are reported separately as a subgroup since 2022 in response to the Clerk's Call to Action; there is no WFA for Black employees because the Act does not designate the subgroup.
Suppression
Counts of 1 to 5 people are hidden in published tables to protect privacy, shown here as "supp." A suppressed cell is not zero.
Promotion equity ratio
A group's share of promotions divided by its share of the workforce. Below 1.0 means the group receives fewer promotions than its size predicts.
Disproportionality ratio
A group's share in a salary band divided by all employees' share in the same band. Above 1.0 in low bands and below 1.0 in high bands signals blocked pay progression.
Acting appointment
Temporarily performing a higher-level job. Acting experience is a common gateway to promotion, which makes equitable access to acting a leading indicator.

Honest limits of this tool

Every number here was transcribed on June 11, 2026 from tables published by the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat in the Employment Equity Annual Report 2024-25 and its Demographic Snapshot, plus the TBS representation and WFA series. Six-band salary counts were produced by summing TBS's published detailed bands and verified against published totals; nothing is estimated, interpolated or modelled. Departmental WFA, departmental promotions and acting appointments, applicant data, subgroup-by-department figures and all PSES results exist only inside interactive federal dashboards and are linked, not copied. Departments below the public-service-wide availability line are screening signals: each department has its own WFA reflecting its occupation and region mix, available inside the PSC dashboard. The disability WFA of 12.0% uses the expanded 2017+ survey definition that the current self-identification form does not, so part of that gap reflects measurement, and TBS expects the modernized self-ID questionnaire to close much of it. Separations include retirements. Legal anchors for action: Employment Equity Act s.5 (duty to identify and eliminate barriers), Canadian Human Rights Act, the Clerk's Call to Action, and the CHRC's 2024 horizontal audit of racialized employment.

Definitions in plain language

The terms used in this tool, in plain language. The technical term is shown in parentheses where it differs.

Employment equity
A legal duty to identify and remove barriers so the workforce reflects the people available to do the work, for the four designated groups.
Designated group
The four groups named in the Employment Equity Act: women, Indigenous Peoples, persons with disabilities, and members of visible minorities (racialized employees).
Subgroup
A more specific group within a designated group, such as First Nations, Métis or Inuit within Indigenous Peoples, or Black employees within racialized employees.
Workforce availability (WFA)
The share of a group in the Canadian workforce available for these jobs, based on the census. It is the benchmark under the Act: a starting point, not a ceiling.
Benchmark
The comparison point a result is measured against. Here it is usually workforce availability.
Representation
The share of employees who have voluntarily self-identified with a group. Because it is voluntary, the true number may be higher.
Representation gap
Representation minus the benchmark, in percentage points. A negative gap means the group is below the level the available workforce would predict.
Suppression
When a count is too small to publish (often 1 to 5 people), it is withheld to protect privacy. A suppressed cell is not zero.
Ratio
One share divided by another. Below 1.0 means less than expected; above 1.0 means more than expected.
Disproportionality index
A group's share within a salary band compared with its share of the whole workforce. Above 1.0 means over-represented in that band; below 1.0, under-represented.
Core public administration (CPA)
The roughly 72 organizations where the Treasury Board is the employer. Separate agencies such as the CRA or Parks Canada report on their own.
Public service
The broader federal public service, including separate agencies. Wider than the core public administration.
Department
A federal organization. Here, an employer covered by the data, used interchangeably with organization.
Public Service Employee Survey (PSES)
A confidential survey of federal employees on their workplace experience, run every one to two years.
Hiring
Bringing a person into a job from outside or through a staffing process, measured here at stages from application to appointment.
Promotion
Moving to a higher-level position. A main path for career progression.
Executive (EX)
The senior leadership group (EX classifications), below the deputy head level.
EX feeder group
The levels just below executive (often EX minus 1 and EX minus 2) from which most executives are drawn.
Self-identification
Voluntarily telling the employer that you belong to a designated group. It is how representation is counted.
Disaggregated data
Data broken down into smaller categories, such as by group, subgroup, level, branch or region, rather than reported as one total.

Limitations of the data

What this public data can and cannot show. Read this before drawing conclusions.

A gap is a signal to investigate, not a final finding. This tool uses language such as "may signal", "may suggest", "should be investigated", and "cannot be concluded from this data alone". It does not state that discrimination has been proven.

What this data does not show

  • Public datasets may not show process-level barriers (who decided what, and how).
  • Suppressed values do not mean zero; they mean the count was too small to publish.
  • Self-identification is voluntary, so representation may understate the true numbers.
  • A department's own workforce availability may differ from the public-service-wide benchmark, reflecting its occupations and region.
  • Data may not include branch, region, classification, occupational group, language profile, security level, or process stage.
  • Some findings require additional departmental data before conclusions can be drawn.
